bet.text: Spend no time lining up: the End Effector's "Flying V" wedge aligns it to the tip of the Reef pipe.
The architecture came from one idea, the fastest cycle possible.

demand.text: Win matches with efficient coral scoring, focused on L3 and L4, that is resilient to defense. Collect ranking points with three or more coral in auto and a deep cage climb, and score algae in the processor to help coopertition.

auto.text: The driver picks a scoring sequence. A* and AD* generate paths around obstacles in real time, and common feeder-to-branch paths are cached when the robot initializes.
Caching saved over 100 ms per path and was needed for five pieces.

cycle.text: Take coral from the floor Intake or the Funnel; the Indexer aligns it into the End Effector. The Elevator goes to level, auto align brings the robot in, the Flying V finds the pipe, and a beam break that detects the pipe triggers the release.
On its practice field it scored 33 to 36 teleop pieces, about 3.8 s each.

endgame.text: The roller claw deploys, its powered wheels grab the deep cage into a latch, and a winch pivots the claw to pull the robot under the cage and off the ground.

fallback.text: The Funnel takes coral from the Coral Station if the Intake breaks.
It was used a lot at Sacramento and East Bay, kept as a failsafe, and not used once at the championship.

gave_up.text: It placed coral with its drivetrain, so it could not strafe in: lateral and heading error had to be in tolerance first, and near the reef it had to back up.
The team says it underestimated algae stealing, with no weight left for a ground algae intake, could score L1 only opposite the ground intake, and wanted more climber space and power.

changed.text: An AlphaBot showed that an end effector without alignment compliance sometimes drops coral. L1 scoring was removed on practice day of the first event and stayed off there.
After the season a team member said they would choose a more traditional end effector, since aligning proved much easier than expected.
After the first event the elevator frame was stiffened and the end effector redesigned.

outcome.text: 42-7-0 in official play; finalist in the Milstein division; ranked 10 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 106.58, Milstein).

solves.text: Accelerate hard on short cycles and resist tipping

facts.text: WCP X2i modules with a 10 tooth X1 reduction; free speed, about
Square frame side
3x1 tubes put the bellypan above the floor by
Motors on the robot
Steel strips stacked inside the bumpers at the rear sides add ballast against tipping
Wheel radius is measured by driving straight and comparing odometry with a tape, because carpet makes it smaller than nominal

cost.text: In a Milstein qualification match a coral bounced off the peg and switched the main breaker off; a breaker guard was added

solves.text: Pick up coral from the floor in any orientation without jamming

cost.text: A 4-bar linkage drives the deploy, but it was not a full 4-bar intake, because the Funnel left no space; so it took much more force from front and side impacts and broke a couple of times at the regionals
Coral jams were a constant thorn through the season, and one came in the Milstein final 2 autonomous
A team member judged it more jammable and breakable than many recent 254 intakes, after chasing weight and tenths of a second instead of the jams
Rubber bands broke fairly often, and the team says they only worked because the foam rollers are compliant
With rollers held by four screws and no adhesive, multiple tubes were destroyed when the intake swept into things
The deploy jackshaft, a 1.25 in tube with 0.03 in wall on custom hubs, was complicated and could not be replaced without pulling a whole mount plate

facts.text: Deploys in about
Roller surface speed, about
Rollers are rubber tubing over foam, for smooth, light, continuous surfaces
The front roller floats on a sprung plate: it opens for long-ways coral and collapses against a wall
Rubber bands act as flat belts that pull coral through dead spots
Front roller in layers: 1/16 in aluminum tube, epoxied 1 in thick open-cell EPDM foam, two layers of gaffers tape wound in opposite directions, 1/32 in silicone
The tape was added after Sacramento, because repeated intaking tore the foam cells and belts deformed the foam
Before the championship the silicone went on by vacuum: pulled out to a 4 in PVC tube, roller slid in, seal broken
Before East Bay the whole intake was pivoted up about 3.5 degrees, so the front roller stopped kicking coral away
The pivots use a tube standoff as a bushing inside a plastic plate, with 2 in fender washers to spread the load

solves.text: Take coral directly from the Coral Station in autonomous, or if the Intake breaks

facts.text: Works with the bumpers this far from the station wall
Steep angle for greater funneling speed
1/32 in polycarbonate stiffened by edge bends and carbon fiber rods
Off-season, it was removed for Chezy Champs for weight, driver visibility and a deeper intake stow

solves.text: Reorient coral from two sources and align it for handoff to the End Effector

facts.text: Eight 4 in flex and star wheels, with cut rims and spokes to prevent jams
Wheel surface speed, about
Two beam breaks, front and rear, inform the state machine

solves.text: Lift the End Effector to all four reef levels and the Barge, stiff enough to place accurately

facts.text: Travel, about
Full travel in about
Two Kraken X60s; 9 mm belts run inside the tubes
A welded A-frame stabilizes it and mounts the Climber
In the redesign, 1/4 in plate crossbars became welded 2x1 tubes, so the fixed stage no longer leaned
A pin through the tube holds each idler pulley at the bottom of a slot in a billet block, kept there by belt tension

cost.text: Before the redesign the end effector swayed at full extension, which slowed the robot, and the bending frame hurt the climb

functions.name: End Effector

solves.text: Place coral without missing or stopping to line up, and handle algae with the same mechanism

cost.text: The design added many constraints (handoff, L1, sensing, not de-scoring, algae, weight), with issues still being fought in the Milstein playoffs
Wrist plates bolted only to the inside faces of the carriage tubes: after much off-season practice the tube ends split, and the team would tie in all faces

functions.type: wristed flex-wheel scorer with a Flying V

facts.text: Wrist rotation
Wrist rotates in about
Coral wheel surface speed, about
Beam breaks position the coral and detect the pipe, which triggers the release
A sprung hoop lets coral pass through for L1 and becomes a hardstop during handoff
A stealth wheel and grippy studs grab algae, on the motor shared with coral
The Flying V was shrunk to save weight to about 6 in wide, about 2 in of working width, and its sides push the end effector over so the coral ends up on the pole
For L1 the wrist pivots off the hardstop and shoots coral out the top, usually landing upright in the trough; two speeds allowed high stacks
The wrist is a 2 in tube with welded end caps on two thin X-contact bearings, with a 1:1 absolute encoder

functions.name: Climber

solves.text: Align to the deep cage and climb it quickly

cost.text: The team says brushing bumpers against an unclimbed partner could lose the climb, and wishes it climbed higher
An A-frame the climber mounts to broke at its short end plugs during a climb at East Bay; longer plugs almost solved it

functions.type: roller claw with latch and winch

facts.text: Two 4 in flex wheels grab the vertical pipe of the cage
A 30 lbf gas spring deploys the claw
The winch sits on the bellypan for a lower center of gravity, on a Kraken X60

The binder calls it a 1:224 gearbox; the team later said the gearbox is only about 11:1, two spur stages, and the rest comes from a 0.5 in hex shaft and a drum of 5.5 in effective diameter at the output
The later figures multiply to about 121:1, so 1:224 stays unexplained
A ratchet and pawl holds the robot up after the match

functions.name: Localization

solves.text: Know the robot's position for auto-align scoring and obstacle avoidance

functions.type: Limelight AprilTag vision with swerve odometry

facts.text: Two Limelight 4s give a MegaTag 1 pose near tags; farther away odometry leads, with periodic vision corrections
It used MegaTag 1 range with gyro bearing unless it saw several tags or was very close, and when scoring only updates that included the tag on that face
The AlphaBot showed cameras must be set back from the corners to see tags near the reef
The two cameras' estimates are fused, weighted by variance, into one before reaching the pose estimator, to save loop time and to keep vision from being overweighted against odometry
Both cameras point straight ahead, and their views overlap on the reef tag until about 5 in from it

cost.text: Limelights needed constant recalibration, because a big collision can shift the lens against the imager
About 5% of the time a Limelight did not connect within a couple of minutes of power-on; a reboot generally fixed it

solves.text: Drive optimized, collision-free paths in autonomous

facts.text: Pre-computed paths are merged with on-the-fly paths
PID control acted about the held coral instead of the robot's center, because that is the point that matters
Robot-relative tracking gave cross-track error its own gain, since it was the less forgiving error at the peg
Paths can slow down while driving, such as when the next coral has not finished staging
Separate limits on forward and sideways acceleration avoid pitch, roll and oscillation with the elevator up

functions.name: Tele-op state machine

solves.text: Let a single driver run every mechanism

functions.type: centralized state machine with driver modes

facts.text: The driver selects coral, manual coral, or algae and climb modes; presets move the Elevator and End Effector together
The published code tracks coral in six states from the indexer and claw sensors, and resets to none when a wait times out
Two CANrange sensors must see clear space before the elevator deploys or stows, with a look ahead at robot speed, in case odometry is lost
When a direct move would collide, the shortest route is picked from transition times generated in simulation
The elevator does not rise without a piece except in manual coral mode, which also frees pieces stuck under it

functions.name: Electronics and CAN
functions.type: two CAN buses on CANivores, with protected sensor power

facts.text: One CANivore serves drivetrain and climber and the other everything else, both in line rather than star topology
Step-up and step-down converters give two protected 12 V rails and one 5 V rail, and most sensors run from the 12 V
Kraken power terminals are tightened past the recommended 0.9 N·m, which loosened over time, to
CAN wires ride on top of power wires where possible, with sleeves and edge tape against sharp edges and hot glue on almost all connections; panels and mounts shield wires from falling coral

cost.text: Another team warns that some of its terminals came off the motor circuit board even at 0.9 N·m

decisions.choice: Passive alignment in the End Effector
decisions.because: it removes time spent lining up and dropped coral
decisions.instead_of: an end effector without alignment compliance, tried on the AlphaBot

decisions.choice: Drive into the reef to score
decisions.because: a scoring motion that coordinates elevator and arm is slower
decisions.instead_of: a pivoting arm, tried on the AlphaBot

decisions.choice: Lift algae and shoot it lightly into the Barge
decisions.because: the team wanted never to miss
the wheel is 2 in wide and grippier, and the azimuth runs on a gear
decisions.instead_of: the SDS MK4i modules of previous years, with a belt azimuth

decisions.choice: Intake on the side opposite scoring
decisions.because: it minimizes the distance and rotations needed

decisions.choice: Keep a Funnel beside the floor Intake
decisions.because: the binder calls it an alternate path for autonomous and redundancy if the Intake breaks; the team later said it came from early tests in which coral stayed near the station, making a human load look fastest, and from wanting the best autonomous
decisions.cost: coral rolled much farther at events and floor loading was faster, but by then removing the Funnel was more work than keeping it

decisions.choice: Remove L1 scoring at the first event
decisions.because: it was not working, and the robot did better than if the team had kept solving it live

decisions.choice: Build an AlphaBot in one week on the 2023 elevator and drivebase
decisions.because: the team wanted to learn gameplay early and give software a robot to develop on
decisions.cost: its fixed ground intake was fragile and got in the way of the cameras, and a funnel handoff was too difficult, so it never gave the autos and early driver practice hoped for

decisions.choice: Cache paths when the robot initializes
decisions.because: it saved over 100 ms per path in autonomous, needed for five pieces

decisions.choice: Stop coral against a physical hardstop in the claw
decisions.because: with a sensor alone coral overshot by varying amounts, and shuffling it back cost time every cycle
decisions.instead_of: a sensor alone, kept now as confirmation

decisions.choice: Silicone over foam rollers on the intake
decisions.because: foam deforms around coral, giving the silicone much more control, and the top roller weighed about 2.5 lb
decisions.instead_of: flex wheels, which would have weighed more, and grip tape, which wore down

decisions.choice: Deploy the intake by a linkage
decisions.because: it is significantly lighter than chain, needs no tensioning or clocking and leaves more freedom to place the jackshaft
decisions.instead_of: chain, or driving the plates at the pivot

decisions.choice: Button head bolt and standoff pivots
decisions.because: shoulder bolts are weak at the undercut and heavy for their strength
it performed better than MegaTag 2, above all at long range and while moving
software has more success with them, and they avoid a separate zeroing sensor and its wiring
decisions.instead_of: the motor's own incremental encoder with a zeroing sensor
